subChunks.title: Genetic Genealogy for Adoptees

storyBeats.txt: The previous lesson, Theodora said, covered the broad landscape of unknown parentage. This one goes deeper into a specific but vast population: people who were formally adopted and are now using DNA to reconstruct what the records concealed.

Adoption as a legal institution is remarkably recent. In England and Wales, it was not legally regulated until 1926. In the United States, individual states began legislating from the 1850s. Before those dates, informal adoption — raising a relative's or neighbour's child as your own — left almost no paper trail at all.

What makes adoptee research distinctly different from general unknown parentage research is scale and system. Tens of millions of adoptions occurred in the twentieth century. Sealed records were the deliberate policy of governments and adoption agencies. The secrets were institutional, not just personal.
DNA does not respect institutional secrecy. It does not know about sealed court records. It simply shows who shares your genome.

subChunks.hookHtml:
Between 1945 and 1975, approximately 1.5 million babies were adopted in the United States alone. In the United Kingdom, over 500,000 adoptions were recorded in the twentieth century. In many cases, original birth records were sealed, biological family members were forbidden from searching, and adoptees were explicitly told their origins could never be known.

Since the rise of consumer DNA testing, those institutional certainties have collapsed. Adoptees who grew up believing they could never find their biological families are now routinely discovering parents, half-siblings, and extended biological kin through DNA matching — sometimes within days of receiving their results. Understanding the specific techniques, challenges, and ethics of adoptee DNA research is essential for any professional or serious genealogist.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Makes Adoptee DNA Research Distinct

In a typical genealogical DNA research project, a person can build their tree on both sides, identify which DNA matches belong to which lines, and use documentary research to fill gaps. Adoptees may have no tree to build from on either biological side. Every match is initially unattributed — it could be maternal or paternal, and there may be no documents at all to anchor the analysis.

This creates specific challenges: (1) no reference points for phasing or attributing matches to a side; (2) emotional complexity (the person being researched may have significant personal investment in the outcome); (3) the possible existence of biological relatives who do not know the adoptee exists, or who do not want to be found.

The Multi-Platform Testing Strategy

Maximising match data is the first priority. Test on AncestryDNA (largest database, especially for UK/US/Irish/Scandinavian ancestry). Transfer raw DNA to MyHeritage (strong European coverage), FamilyTreeDNA (has chromosome browser and full mtDNA/Y-DNA options), and upload to GEDmatch (cross-platform comparison, triangulation tools). Each database will return unique matches not found elsewhere.

If the adoptee is male, testing Y-DNA through FamilyTreeDNA provides a direct patrilineal line — haplogroup and surname project matching may indicate paternal surname. Full mtDNA testing traces the direct maternal line, though the genealogical timeframe is uncertain without close matches.

Interpreting the Match List: Side Attribution

Without parents tested, attributing matches to maternal or paternal side is the central challenge. Methods include:

  • Leeds Method clustering: Assigns matches into four grandparent clusters. Even without side attribution, patterns of cluster overlap reveal which clusters may be related (i.e., both paternal) vs. independent (maternal vs. paternal).
  • Shared match analysis: If two matches share each other but not a third match, they likely descend from the same side. Building trees for the highest matches in each apparent cluster and looking for a common ancestral couple identifies the relevant family.
  • Half-sibling or close relative as anchor: If a half-sibling (sharing one biological parent) tests and is identified, all of their shared matches with the adoptee can be attributed to the shared parent's side, leaving the remaining matches attributable to the other parent.

Building the Candidate Parent Profile

Once a biological family network is identified (through clustering and tree-building), the next step is identifying the specific individual most likely to be the biological parent. Criteria include: age at time of adoptee's birth (must be biologically plausible — typically 15–45 for mothers, 15–75 for fathers); geography (was the person in the right place at the right time?); marital status at time of birth (unmarried status was frequently associated with adoption placement in the mid-20th century); and consistency with any non-identifying information provided to the adoptee by the adoption agency.

Non-Identifying Information

Many adoption agencies and local authorities hold non-identifying information — background details about the biological family that have been stripped of names and identifying specifics. This may include: birth mother's age at time of placement; her occupation and education; siblings; medical history; reason for placement; and physical description. This information can be invaluable for narrowing a candidate list once DNA has identified a family group.

In England and Wales, non-identifying information can be requested from the adoption agency or local authority that handled the adoption. In Scotland, the Adoption Register Scotland holds records. In the US, processes vary by state — many adoption agencies still hold records and will release non-identifying information on request.

DNA Matching for International Adoptions

International adoptions — particularly from China (1990s–2000s), South Korea (1950s–present), Romania (1990s), and Guatemala (2000s) — present additional challenges. Match databases have limited coverage for East Asian, Southeast Asian, and Eastern European populations. FamilyTreeDNA has stronger East Asian representation than Ancestry for some populations. The China Roots project specifically assists Korean and Chinese adoptees. Language barriers and record access restrictions in the country of birth add complexity.

For Korean adoptees, the GeneBase Korea project on FamilyTreeDNA and the Korean DNA Project aim to expand the reference database. DNA Consultants and similar services offer ancestry-by-population analysis that can confirm ethnic origins even where family matching is sparse.

The Role of Social Media

DNA matching identifies the family; social media can help identify specific individuals. Family surname groups on Facebook, LinkedIn profiles, local history pages, and obituary sites (Legacy.com, Findagrave) can all help identify which member of a known biological family is most likely to be the biological parent. This work must be conducted with care — reading publicly available information is legitimate; creating false identities to gather information is not.

When the Biological Parent Does Not Want Contact

The Mutual Consent Voluntary Register (England/Wales, administered by local authorities and the GRO) allows biological relatives to register their willingness to make contact. NORCAP (Now After Adoption) and the Post Adoption Centre provide intermediary services for facilitated contact and rejection handling. Some biological parents specifically indicate through intermediary services that they do not want contact — this must be respected, even though DNA evidence has established the relationship beyond doubt.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old how someone who was adopted as a baby and has no documents at all can use DNA to find their biological family — even if neither biological parent has ever done a DNA test.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: Maria was adopted in England in 1968. She has no non-identifying information and her original birth certificate shows only 'mother: Margaret Jones' with no father listed. She has tested on AncestryDNA and received the following top matches: (1) a predicted second cousin at 320 cM whose tree shows the Hartley and Baines families in West Yorkshire; (2) a predicted second cousin once removed at 190 cM sharing many of the same Hartley matches; (3) a separate cluster of matches around 150–200 cM with trees showing the Nolan and Reilly families in County Mayo, Ireland. Describe the initial analytical steps you would take and what additional tests or research would help resolve which side is maternal and which is paternal.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The clustering pattern already suggests two distinct family networks: a West Yorkshire cluster (Hartley/Baines) and an Irish cluster (Nolan/Reilly). These are likely the two biological parent sides.

Steps: Apply Leeds Method to all matches to confirm the cluster boundaries and identify any overlapping matches. Build trees for the two highest-cM matches in each cluster to identify their most recent common ancestors with each other. This gives approximate generation depths for each family.

To identify the biological mother: the birth certificate names 'Margaret Jones' as mother — this is a starting point. Research the West Yorkshire Hartley family tree forward to women of appropriate age (born c.1940–1955 to be Maria's mother at 1968 birth). Cross-reference any women named Margaret in this family group. Similarly investigate the Irish Nolan/Reilly network for a potential father.

Additional tests: If any of Maria's DNA matches have a parent or grandparent tested, examine their shared match patterns to further confirm cluster attributions. Y-DNA testing is not applicable (Maria is female), but could be offered to a male biological relative if one is identified and willing. Request non-identifying information from the adoption agency if available.

Ultimately, documentary verification of the candidate biological mother — confirming her birth (GRO), her presence in England around 1967–1968, and any address connection to the adoption placement area — should corroborate the DNA evidence before any contact is considered.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A Chinese adoptee, born in 1997 and adopted by a British family from Hunan Province at age 2, wants to find her biological family. She has tested on AncestryDNA and MyHeritage. Her highest match is a predicted fourth cousin at 67 cM with a Chinese-American tree; all other matches are below 30 cM. Discuss the challenges specific to this research scenario and what additional strategies — including non-DNA approaches — might help.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
This case illustrates the limitations of current genealogical DNA databases for non-Western populations. Chinese citizens have tested on genealogical platforms at far lower rates than British or American populations, meaning the match list will be sparse and distant. The highest match at 67 cM (predicted 4th cousin) is a weak anchor — the relationship range for 67 cM includes 3rd cousin twice removed, half-4th cousin, and more, meaning the shared ancestral couple could be several generations back.

Additional DNA strategies: Upload raw DNA to FamilyTreeDNA (stronger East Asian representation in some haplogroup projects); consider the China Roots project specifically aimed at this population; upload to GEDmatch for cross-platform matching. CRI Genetics and DNA Consultants offer ancestral population admixture analysis that can at minimum confirm provincial origin from broader Chinese reference populations — Hunan ancestry may show distinct admixture patterns from other provinces.

Non-DNA approaches: The adoption was in 1997 from Hunan — the one-child policy era. Many Chinese adoptees were abandoned (often girls, due to cultural son preference combined with the one-child policy). Chinese adoption files sometimes include finding ads — newspaper announcements of a foundling child, published by the institution before the adoption. These occasionally carry location information. The adoptive family's adoption agency may hold non-identifying information. Some Chinese adoptees have had success through Chinese social media platforms (WeChat, Weibo) posting family search requests using official government channels. The Hunan provincial DNA database for missing persons is occasionally used by families seeking lost children from this era.

The emotional dimension is particularly complex: biological parents may have abandoned the child under duress (government pressure, poverty, gender preference) and carry significant guilt or grief. The researcher should be prepared to help the client navigate the possibility that biological family members may be found but reluctant to engage openly.
learningObjectives: Explain the specific challenges that make adoptee DNA research distinct from general genealogical DNA analysis.
Describe the multi-platform testing strategy and why testing on a single platform is insufficient.
Apply Leeds Method clustering and shared match analysis to attribute matches to maternal or paternal sides without a reference parent.
Identify the sources of non-identifying information available to adoptees in England and Wales.
commonMistakes: Testing only on AncestryDNA and assuming all relevant matches will be found there — unique matches exist in every platform.
Treating a 'predicted second cousin' relationship as definitive — cM ranges overlap significantly with other relationship types.
Approaching biological relatives directly without considering whether they may be unaware of the adoptee's existence.
Failing to request non-identifying information from the adoption agency, which can significantly narrow candidate lists from DNA research.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies the distinct challenges of adoptee DNA research including lack of documentary anchors and emotional complexity.
Describes the multi-platform approach and Leeds Method clustering with sufficient specificity to apply them.
Demonstrates understanding of the legal and institutional landscape for adoptee record access in England and Wales.
Shows appropriate ethical sensitivity in approaches to biological relative contact and international adoption complexities.

UK organisation providing intermediary services for adoptees and biological relatives seeking contact, including cases where one party does not want contact.

FamilyTreeDNA-affiliated project aiming to expand the genealogical DNA database for East Asian populations, particularly useful for Chinese and Korean adoptees.

China's 1980–2015 one-child policy led to widespread abandonment of female infants; finding ads published in local newspapers are sometimes available and carry location information about abandoned children.

questions.questionHtml: What is 'non-identifying information' in the context of adoption research?
options: DNA data stripped of haplogroup classifications
Background details about the biological family released without names or identifying specifics
Adoption court records that have been officially anonymised by the court
Census records where the adoptee appears under their adoptive family's surname
questions.correctAnswer: Background details about the biological family released without names or identifying specifics
questions.explanationHtml: Non-identifying information includes biological parents' ages, occupations, health history, reason for placement, and physical descriptions — everything that contextualises the adoption without enabling direct identification. It is often held by adoption agencies and local authorities.

questions.questionHtml: An adoptee has tested on AncestryDNA and has two distinct clusters of matches: one showing Yorkshire surnames, one showing Irish surnames. She has no tested parent or sibling. What is the most logical first conclusion about these two clusters?
options: Both clusters are on the same (maternal) side since they both appear in the same database
The two clusters likely represent the two biological parent sides — one maternal and one paternal family network
The clusters should be merged since all of her DNA came from two people
The Irish cluster is probably an error since Irish genealogy is notoriously poorly represented
questions.correctAnswer: The two clusters likely represent the two biological parent sides — one maternal and one paternal family network
questions.explanationHtml: When Leeds Method clustering produces two distinct family networks with no evident connection to each other, these most likely represent the two biological parent lineages. Further tree-building for each cluster will help identify which is maternal and which is paternal.

questions.questionHtml: Why is multi-platform DNA testing especially important for adoptees compared to non-adoptee genealogists?
options: Adoptees receive inaccurate results on individual platforms due to lack of reference data
Adoptees cannot transfer raw DNA between platforms, so must test independently on each
With no documentary tree to anchor analysis, maximising the match pool is critical — every platform holds unique matches not found elsewhere
Platforms penalise adoptees by placing them in lower-confidence result tiers
questions.correctAnswer: With no documentary tree to anchor analysis, maximising the match pool is critical — every platform holds unique matches not found elsewhere
questions.explanationHtml: Adoptees have no existing documentary tree to cross-reference, so every DNA match is potential evidence. Since no single platform has universal coverage, testing or uploading to multiple platforms (Ancestry, MyHeritage, FTDNA, GEDmatch) significantly increases the probability of finding a close enough match to anchor the research.
